Sandia report SAND2026-25421, by Amanda K. Jones, surveys the Hawaiian hoary bat at the lab's Kauai Test Facility. The bat is the only bat species expected in the area, the report notes. Acoustic recorders captured bat calls at set sites.

Software called Kaleidoscope sorts calls by amplitude, shape, length, and frequency. Any call classed as a bat was credited to this species. Noise files were tallied separately from bat calls at each site. The species code LASCIN labels the bat in the data. Facility managers learn when bats use the site, guiding work timing.
doe-osti-3914962-facilitating-connection:
Paige Skur and Denise Barber of the National Laboratory of the Rockies wrote this September 2026 report, NLR/TP-6A50-98547, on the American-Made Network. The Energy Department set up the American-Made program in 2018 to fund new energy ideas through prizes and contests, not just grants. The Network branch links prize teams with skilled helpers across industry.

The report explains how those links work in practice. Network members called Power Connectors coach teams, open doors to experts, and share hard-won know-how. One case follows Jade Garrett of Positive Deviancy, who backed more than 450 teams across 63 prizes in seven years. Readers get a clear view of how a prize program can give small teams reach they could not build alone.
experimental-determination-of-the-veloci:
Michelson's Experimental Determination of the Velocity of Light reports his early precision measurement at Annapolis. Albert A. Michelson was then a Master in the United States Navy. The work was done at the U.S. Naval Academy at private expense. Simon Newcomb's note of February 20, 1880, frames the paper.

Newcomb links light speed to finding the solar parallax by the best method then known. The contents lay out the theory of Michelson's new method first. Apparatus and constants follow, then formulas and grouped observations. Separate results, error discussion, and objections fill the later sections. Michelson takes sole credit and responsibility, Newcomb stresses. The paper marks a young officer's entry into exact physical measurement.
frank-on-a-gun-boat:
Castlemon's Frank Nelson enlists in the Navy and learns the ropes aboard a river gunboat. The Gun-Boat Series chapters promise a midnight alarm, a discomfited rebel, capture, and an escape chased by blood-hounds. A faithful friend and a spunky rebel share the adventures.

Taken prisoner, Frank is confined in the lower part of a fort, directly in range of the iron-clads' shells. He expects to be struck every moment as the pieces fly about him. He knows the rebels cherish an especial hatred toward gun-boatmen. Harry Castlemon published Frank on a Gun-Boat in 1892, decades after the war that made his name.
frus-1952-54Guat:
Guatemala from 1952 to 1954 fills this retrospective volume, a documentary history of PBSUCCESS. The CIA operation ended with the 1954 coup that removed President Jacobo Arbenz from power. Agency files form the core of the record.

An earlier plan, PBFORTUNE, first weighed in 1951, appears in the sources note. The main run then tracks the operation as built and run. A third project, PBHISTORY, mined the fallen government's papers. Cryptonyms and pseudonyms fill the lists. The volume is a rare inside view of a covert action, from first pitch to final use of captured files.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DoleRobertSenat: Howard Kurtz, the Washington Post's media writer, examined how the press covered what the headline calls the Dole Affair, involving Senator Robert Dole. His piece, Behind the Scenes, looks at the reporting itself rather than at the underlying events. The surviving record gives the author, paper, and subject, but no date or findings, so the article stands as an example of Kurtz's media criticism from his Post years.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KautenMarieMat_: Harold Weisberg wrote to Mr. and Mrs. Kauten on January 22, 1977. The archive's entry gives the correspondents and the date and nothing of the contents. Weisberg's letters went out by the thousands, to sources, readers, and friends of his work. This one stands as a single dated entry in that correspondence, its subject unrecorded.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ODanielPat_ODan:
The Dallas Times Herald reported on March 19, 1968, that Pat O'Daniel wanted a state investigation of President Kennedy's assassination. O'Daniel was then a candidate for governor of Texas. His call asked Texas to run its own inquiry, five years after the shooting and four after the Warren Report.

Demands for a new inquiry were a constant of the case's politics. Most came from private critics; O'Daniel's came from a man running for office in the state where the crime occurred. The article records his request and its setting in the 1968 campaign. It shows the assassination still working as live politics in Texas, not merely as history argued in books.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WatergateSpoofs: Tom Huth reported for the Washington Post on a strange Watergate side business: anti-Nixon novelties were selling fast. Even during a television recess in the hearings, vendors found buyers for jokes at the president's expense. Huth's article treats the trade as news about the public mood. When a scandal becomes souvenirs, anger and humor are clearly sharing the same street.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Th:
Fifty years after the scandal broke, this briefing book, number 870, looks back at the CIA's secret role in Chile. Peter Kornbluh edited it, and it was published on September 9, 2024. Its documents center on Henry Kissinger and what he told people about that role.

The records show Kissinger misled the president, the cabinet, and reporters about CIA activity in Chile. He told journalist Ted Koppel the issue was total nonsense, even as a New York Times exposé sent the White House into anger and panic. A secret White House memo captured his view that America should not let a country go communist.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba_The:
Fifty-five years after the Cuban Missile Crisis, William Burr and Peter Kornbluh edited this briefing book, number 606, published in October 2017. It gathers papers on parts of the crisis that planning documents reveal. One is an occupation proclamation drafted for Cuba.

The proclamation ordered all persons in occupied territory to obey all orders promptly. It was written for an invasion that never came. CIA post-mortems also admitted a photo-gap on missile sites, caused by limits placed on U-2 spy flights. Together the papers show how close Washington came to occupying Cuba, and how blind spots shaped the crisis.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
In April 1995 Russian forces destroyed the Chechen village of Samashki, killing many civilians. Svetlana Savranskaya and Matthew Evangelista edited this briefing book, number 702, published in April 2020. It examines the massacre and the American response to Russia's war in Chechnya.

The pairing of the two presidents in the title is the analytical point. Boris Yeltsin's Russia was then a partner the Clinton administration wanted to keep, which shaped how Washington reacted to atrocity reports. Documents on the response let readers weigh friendship against evidence. The Samashki case became a test of whether the new post-Cold War relationship had room for human rights pressure.

During the Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962, Soviet submarines carrying nuclear torpedoes were being hunted by American ships above them. Sixty years later, this National Security Archive posting gathers the core declassified records on those submarines and on how close one of them came to firing its nuclear weapon.

At a 1997 conference, brigade chief of staff Vasili Arkhipov gave signs that confirmed the near-use of a nuclear torpedo aboard his submarine. The commanders involved had kept the story quiet for forty years. The records here let readers piece together the underwater half of the crisis, a part long hidden even while the standoff between Kennedy and Khrushchev above the surface became famous.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cuba_Luis_Posada_: Luis Posada Carriles, the Cuban exile militant who spent decades in the CIA's orbit and was accused of bombing a Cuban airliner in 1976, died at ninety. A National Security Archive briefing book page carries his obituary under a headline drawn from the agency's own reported phrase for him: a CIA-created Frankenstein, a asset who escaped his makers' control. Posada was never convicted for the bombing and lived his last years in Miami. Only the page capture survives here, marking the Archive's notice of a violent Cold War life.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_Freedom_of_I:
President Lyndon Johnson signed the Freedom of Information Act with reluctance in 1966, and the law turned sixty in July 2026. A National Security Archive posting marked the anniversary by calling the act a national transparency treasure: the tool that lets Americans request, obtain, and study the records of their own government.

Few organizations have used FOIA more than the Archive itself, whose lawsuits and requests built much of the public record on modern American foreign policy. An anniversary piece from that source doubles as a user's report on what the law has achieved and where it strains, in delays and denials. Readers get a short history of a statute that quietly underpins a great deal of reporting, scholarship, and public argument.
if-not-silver-what:
John W. Bookwalter, a maker and land owner from Ohio, argued the money question in this 1896 book. He opens with a speech by A. J. Balfour against a gold standard that keeps rising in value. Bookwalter says his farm-linked trade forced him to study coinage at home and abroad.

His case favors silver and a double standard of gold and silver. He traces past panics, bank strain in England, and the role of France in holding both metals. Farmers and makers, he holds, bear the cost when money grows scarce. The book is a plain brief from the silver side.
island-tales-on-the-makaloa-mat:
Jack London set the seven stories of On the Makaloa Mat in Hawaii, and the collection appeared in 1920, after his death. The title story opens on Martha Scandwell, a wealthy Waikiki matriarch under her great hau tree, telling tales of the old islands. Other stories take up the bones of the chief Kahekili, a Chinese servant's tears, surfing, and the memories of old Hawaiians.

London mixes plantation wealth with native legend, and the races of modern Honolulu crowd his pages: Japanese servants, Chinese nurses, haole fortunes, and kanaka storytellers. His Hawaii is beautiful and haunted at once. Readers who know London for dogs and snow will find the same strong storytelling working in heat and surf.
life-history-of-the-kangaroo-rat:
Charles T. Vorhies and Walter P. Taylor wrote this 1922 government bulletin. The Agriculture Department issued it as Bulletin Number 1091. Arizona's Agricultural Experiment Station shared in the work. Its subject is the banner-tailed kangaroo rat of the Southwest.

Chapters cover identification, occurrence, habits, food, and burrow systems. The authors also study the rat's commensals, enemies, and abundance. Economic considerations close the report for farmers and ranchers. Forty pages of close observation make it a model species life history. Plates show the banner-tailed kangaroo rat in its desert home. A forty-item bibliography supports the authors' field observations.
lights-and-shadows-of-new-york-life-or-t:
James D. McCabe Jr. describes New York in all its phases here. The National Publishing Company sold the book by subscription only. Its subtitle promises the great city's sights and sensations. Engravings show noted places, life, and scenes throughout.

McCabe promises accounts of splendors and wretchedness alike. Marble palaces and dark dens stand side by side in his plan. Rings, frauds, charities, mysteries, and crimes all receive coverage. Leading men, politicians, and adventurers complete his city portrait. Grand Central Railway Depot illustrates the subscription prospectus handsomely. Agents called on residents who wrote the publishers for copies.
mauprat:
George Sand's novel Mauprat appears here in Stanley Young's English version. Front essays tell of Sand's life and of her place in letters. Edmund Gosse wrote the life, and the author's own preface follows.

One essay calls Sand the greatest woman writer the world has known. It praises her candor, her free spirit, and her warm heart. Her foes, it says, feared her warnings and her plain truth. The tale itself bears her famed pen name, George Sand, on its title page. The preface by the author stands just before the tale starts. Life, praise, and the tale itself give three views of one writer.
mob-rule-in-new-orleans-robert-charles-a:
Ida B. Wells-Barnett published this pamphlet in 1900, interrupting a larger work to write it. A mob in New Orleans had roamed the streets day and night. Its members beat, shot, and killed Black residents at will, despising all law. Wells-Barnett tells the story of Robert Charles and his fight to the death.

She builds her account from the New Orleans Times-Democrat and Picayune. Both papers, she notes, condemned the mob and defended law and order. The pamphlet also prints lynching statistics and recalls the burning of Sam Hose in Georgia. Wells-Barnett shows he killed his employer in self-defense, not in crime.
nasa-tm-19640023646-an-ultraviolet-spect:
Kenneth Hallam and John Mangus of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this paper. They presented it at a Tokyo optics meeting on September 1, 1964. It describes a tool for studying ultraviolet light from space. The tool was built for OSO-B, the second Orbiting Solar Observatory.

A spectrophotometer splits light into its colors and measures each part. This one was meant to analyze ultraviolet output from stars and nebulae. Its slit sits at the focus of a six-inch reflecting telescope. Earth's air blocks ultraviolet light, so the tool had to fly. The paper details a key early step toward space-based ultraviolet astronomy.
nasa-tm-19650003085-stability-and-contro:
M Leroy Spearman and Gerald V Foster tested a swing-wing aircraft shape in the Langley supersonic pressure tunnel. The outer wing panels were swept back seventy-five degrees. Testing ran at Mach 2.01, just over twice the speed of sound.

Their summary reports a fairly straight-line change in pitching moment as lift rose. That meant the static margin could fall to about five percent at low lift before the shape turned neutrally stable. In plain terms, the swept shape stayed predictable at high speed. Such results guided later variable-sweep designs.
nasa-tm-19650025631-a-summary-of-hingele:
John F Ward and a Langley colleague summarized research on helicopter rotors built with no hinges, in a report whose scan is partly garbled. A normal rotor blade flaps on hinges as it turns. A hingeless rotor instead flexes as one stiff structure. Langley work included an early flight test program using a three-blade hingeless rotor fitted to a helicopter.

Wind tunnel testing of a scaled research model formed the second strand of the work. Such rotors promise simpler hubs and sharper control response for the pilot. They also raise hard questions about loads and vibration in the blades. The summary gathers the flight and tunnel strands in one place, so rotor designers could weigh the gains against the costs.
nasa-tm-19660008283-an-analysis-of-the-t:
Robert Siegel and Joseph M Savino at Lewis Research Center analyzed a freezing problem with many uses, in a paper offered for an August 1966 heat meeting in Chicago. A warm liquid flows over a wall that is cooled from the other side. A frozen layer grows on the wall as the liquid passes. The growth changes with time, which is what transient means here.

The frozen layer insulates the wall as it thickens. That slows further freezing in a self-limiting way. Flows of this kind appear in casting, in cooling systems, and in fuel handling. Siegel and Savino give an analysis that predicts the layer's growth, so engineers need not rely on trial and error alone.
nasa-tm-19660015112-a-lunar-ephemeris-wi:
Theodore L Felsentreger at Goddard published a lunar ephemeris in March 1966 with an unusual reference frame. An ephemeris is a table of positions over time. Felsentreger gives the Moon's positions referred to Earth's equatorial plane. Most tables of the era used a different plane. His choice suits users who work in Earth-based coordinates, such as tracking stations and orbit computers.

Daily motions of the Moon's angular orbital elements are part of the work, per the catalog note. Apollo planning made precise lunar positions a daily need. A table in the user's own frame saves conversion errors. Felsentreger's ephemeris served the missions then being prepared, when the Moon was about to become a workplace.
nasa-tm-19660024047-stability-and-contro:
Ross B Robinson and M Leroy Spearman tested a lightweight glider reentry shape in Langley's four by four foot supersonic pressure tunnel. Testing ran at Mach 1.89, just under twice the speed of sound. The shape was an all-wing design with a diamond planform. A small fuselage sat on top of the wing, the summary says. Flight attitudes studied were those of normal flight in the air, at fairly low angles of attack.

A glider that returns from space must fly well at both extremes of its journey. Supersonic stability and control in the air are the middle part of that problem. Robinson and Spearman report the characteristics measured for this diamond-wing layout. Lightweight glider concepts were a leading alternative to capsules in that period of reentry research.
nasa-tm-19660029426-a-theoretical-and-ex:
Charles Borden Johnson wrote this work as a master's thesis in aerospace engineering at the Virginia Polytechnic Institute in August 1966. His test case is a flat plate fitted with a flap at its trailing edge. The plate flies, in a wind tunnel, at Mach 8, eight times the speed of sound.

Johnson combined theory with experiment. He measured how the pressure spread across the plate and how the flow separated near the deflected flap. He varied the Reynolds number, the flap angle, and the wall temperature to see each effect. Flow separation at such speeds matters for vehicles that fly in the upper atmosphere.
nasa-tm-19670001914-nasa-selective-disse:
Gifford A. Young, of the Scientific and Technical Information Division at NASA headquarters in Washington, D.C., wrote this program description in June 1966. It explains NASA's selective dissemination of information program, an early computer system for matching new documents to the interests of individual researchers. The system ran on the IBM 7090/94 computer.

Twice each month, the system compared more than 2,000 documents against the stated interests of over 700 participants. Those users sat at ten NASA centers and eleven Air Force centers. Interest profiles could use single key words, short phrases, excluded terms, and percentage matching. Output came as abstract cards, with a response card for requesting full texts. The report covers operating experience, program changes, and availability, and notes a move to newer IBM machines in February 1966.
nasa-tm-19670005589-low-torque-three-pie:
Report TR-426, issued on September 15, 1966, by the Directorate for Design Engineering at NASA's Kennedy Space Center. It covers a three-piece valve seat built for high-pressure pneumatic valving. A valve seat is the surface a valve closes against to seal. This design aimed to seal well while needing little turning force to operate.

Three different materials served as seating rings during qualification testing. The test series included water proof tests, pneumatic proof tests, repeated cycle tests, and seat erosion tests. Pressures ran from 6,000 to 10,000 pounds per square inch. All three materials performed satisfactorily across that range. The report concludes that, for design purposes, the choice among the seating materials is not particularly critical.
nasa-tm-19670013515-communications-syste:
H. E. Smith, of the Manufacturing Engineering Laboratory at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, wrote this memorandum on December 6, 1966. Astronauts trained for weightlessness underwater, floating in tanks that simulate zero gravity. Crews in and around the tank needed to talk to each other clearly.

Smith describes a two-way communications system built for that training. It connects nine personnel stations and a public address system. Underwater speakers let the safety divers hear what is said. The report also gives operating instructions for the system, so training crews could run it day to day.
nasa-tm-19700014017-the-as-205-csm-101-l:
Gordon W. Solomon of the Marshall Space Flight Center prepared this data report on September 10, 1968. It gives the planned flight path for the AS-205 launch vehicle carrying the CSM-101 spacecraft. The volume is Revision 1 of the operational trajectory, the working path planners expected the flight to follow.

Solomon lays out the predicted path, the mission goals, the ground rules, and a tracking summary. The plan placed the S-IVB stage and spacecraft into a low elliptical orbit, one hundred twenty by one hundred fifty nautical miles up. Later sections cover vehicle traits, guidance and control, powered flight, and the spent stage. The flight would further check launch vehicle and spacecraft systems in orbit.
nasa-tm-19700016330-irradiation-effect-a:
Charles L. Younger and Fred A. Haley of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 meeting on radiation effects in materials. It studies what radiation does to titanium and titanium-base alloys at very low temperatures. The property at issue is tensile strength, how the metal acts when pulled.

Metals in space and nuclear service face both deep cold and steady radiation. The authors test how the two act together on these alloys. Builders need such data to know if a part will stay strong in service. A metal that turns brittle in cold, irradiated use can fail without warning.
nasa-tm-19700025035-investigation-of-lan:
NASA issued this Apollo working paper, number 1180, from the Manned Spacecraft Center program. It investigates a change of landing site during the second phase of the lunar module's powered descent. The change would be made using the primary guidance system, while the craft was already flying down toward the surface.

The calculations ask how much landing area stays open to the crew at that late stage. They track how guidance commands, pitch angle, and thrust would change for an alternate site. Charts show the reachable footprint from three different ranges during the descent. A closing section weighs whether the crew could still see the new landing site well enough to use it.
nasa-tm-19700025124-radiation-pattern-ca:
R. Miezis and R. F. Schmidt of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in June 1970. It gives radiation pattern calculations for the ATS-F antenna. The antenna was a deployable reflector made of forty-eight panels that would unfold in orbit, far too large to launch already open.

The work begins with two ways of finding the reflector's surface normals, one analytic and one numerical. It then builds up the computing steps: small area pieces, numerical integration, and the program's input and output quantities. Notes on computer requirements and critical program areas follow. The closing section presents the computed results for ATS-F itself, the patterns the finished antenna was expected to beam out.
nasa-tm-19700026419-circumlunar-comminic:
John T. McNeeley and Ellis W. Henry of the Advanced Mission Design Branch wrote this internal note on June 20, 1968. It was issued by the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston. It studies radio contact around the Moon using two satellites in lunar polar orbit, passing over both poles as they circle.

The note first fixes the orbit layout the two relay satellites would fly. Deployment and phasing come next, so the pair would stay spaced as the plan requires. Guidance needs, orbit lifetime, and the speed changes required are worked through in turn. A table reports the communication coverage the two satellites could achieve, counted in tracking intervals and percentages.
nasa-tm-19700026436-an-analysis-of-point:
Houston's Manned Spacecraft Center issued this analysis of point-to-point communication for the lunar flyer program. The flyer was a proposed small craft for moving astronauts across the Moon's surface. Radio links between two points on that surface were the problem at hand, especially near the edge of direct sight.

The study seeks the best radio frequency for links near the line-of-sight horizon. It assumes a small transmitter and works through two antenna heights for the link. Losses counted in the circuit budget include free-space loss and diffraction loss where the lunar surface blocks the path. Ground proximity loss, antenna gains, and receiver sensitivity each get a short explanation before the comparison.
nasa-tm-19700032536-contact-resistance-o:
T. H. Wilkinson of the Marshall Space Flight Center ran the tests reported in this technical memorandum. It measures the contact resistance of electroplated conductors in flat conductor cable. Low resistance at each contact keeps signals clean and power losses small.

Three kinds of conductor were tested in a special receptacle. They were gold over nickel plate, cleaned nickel plate, and uncleaned nickel plate. Tests ran indoors, outdoors in winter cold, and after hundreds of mating cycles. The gold-plated contacts showed the lowest resistance, the report states. Cleaned nickel contacts still fell within the acceptable limits.
nasa-tm-19710019413-virtual-image-displa:
An Ames Research Center memorandum, NASA TM X-2327, reports a simple way to make flight simulator scenes look far away. Cheap uncorrected plastic lenses formed a virtual image of the flight scene. A virtual image seems to sit at a real distance, not on a nearby screen. That depth cue makes landings in a simulator feel far more realistic.

Pilots flew takeoffs and landings to judge one setup in practice. It paired a Schmidt color projector and rear screen with one large plastic lens. A second setup used a color television monitor and two lenses. The study varied lens traits to see their effect. Simple lenses, with stated limits, gave a usable scene both ways.
nasa-tm-19710064980-stability-and-contro:
Dewey E Wornom of the Langley Research Center reported force tests of a supersonic target drone model, as Technical Memorandum X-457. The model flew through the Langley eight foot transonic pressure tunnel. Target drones give gunners and missile crews a realistic practice target. This design had movable tail surfaces that could deflect unevenly, left against right, for roll control.

Tests ran from Mach 0.50 to Mach 1.20 across wide angle ranges. The model stayed stable lengthwise and sideways throughout. The movable tails gave strong pitch control, and uneven deflection gave strong roll control. The rudder steered well, though its power halved at the top speed. One caution stood out. Uneven tail deflection also made possibly excessive yaw.
nasa-tm-19720003244-apollo-galactic-x-ra:
I Adler and colleagues issued this preliminary science report in October 1971 on Apollo galactic X-ray observations. It studies how pulsating X-ray sources in our galaxy change over time. NASA's first X-ray satellite, Uhuru, had just found fast flickering in several sources. The pulsations rose and fell on short time scales. Apollo instruments offered another chance to watch that behavior.

The catalog record calls the work a detailed study of that time behavior. Pulsing sources were thought to be compact objects pulling in gas. Their flicker patterns reveal sizes and spin rates that telescopes cannot image directly. Reports like this one belong to the first years of X-ray astronomy. Every new source behavior tested the young field's ideas.
nasa-tm-19720007418-cyclotron-production:
V J Sodd and colleagues evaluated ways to make iodine 123 in this October 1970 report, BRH/DMRE 70-4. It comes from the Bureau of Radiological Health in the United States Public Health Service. Iodine 123 is a radioactive tracer used in medical imaging. It gives patients a low radiation dose compared with older tracers. A cyclotron can produce it through several different nuclear reactions.

The report weighs each production route on its merits. Some reactions make the isotope directly in the target. Others make a parent isotope that later decays into iodine 123. That indirect path runs through a natural precursor. The evaluation runs to forty five pages. Hospitals and producers could use it to pick a practical supply method.
nothing-to-eat:
Horatio Alger and Thomas Chandler Haliburton are named as makers of Nothing to Eat, a comic piece printed in New York in 1857. Its title page stresses that it is not by the author of Nothing to Wear. Pictures go with the verse. A jolly good natured author, it says, dedicates it to all ladies dying with dyspepsia.

Verses up front nibble at appetite and fine dinners: a side bone, dressing, and a bit of the breast. The contents list the argument, the proof under the Queen of Fashion, and the object aimed at. Fashion and folly, says a tag, are all of a suit. The poem mocks grand dinners where a guest finds nothing to eat.
private-peat:
Harold R. Peat, a former soldier of the Third Battalion of the First Canadian Contingent, wrote a memoir of the Great War printed in New York in 1917. Photographs taken at the front fill the book, along with scenes from a photo-play of the same name.

Chapters run from the call to arms and training in the old country to life under fire and a figure the men called the Mad Major. Peat lost the use of his right arm, yet the tone stays cheerful. Readers get a plain soldier's view of the trenches, told with humour.
ptomaine-street-the-tale-of-warble-petti:
Carolyn Wells wrote a comic tale in verse about Warble Petticoat and called it, in her foreword, a foolish book. The foreword itself is a rhymed romp, quoting poets who praised folly and noting that fools, by old saying, rush in where angels fear to tread.

Wells asks only for the reader's gentle smile to egg her wit on, and warns that the mirth may not be worth the price of white paper. What follows keeps that promise of nonsense over sense. Readers get light verse, wordplay, and a tale told for laughs rather than lessons.
the-adventure-club-afloat:
Ralph Henry Barbour wrote The Adventure Club Afloat in 1917, a boys' tale with art by E. C. Caswell, given by Barbour to H. P. Holt with a joke about stolen thunder. Chapter one, How It Started, goes back to the club's birth.

On a warm June night in Number 17 Sumner Hall, the oldest and most vine-hung dorm at Dexter Academy, three boys lounge in low gas light. Exams ended that day and graduation sits just twenty-eight hours off, so none does more than yawn. From that idle talk a plan for a summer cruise is born. Readers get schoolboy friends, motor cruisers, and coastal scrapes in Barbour's clean, brisk style.
the-adventures-of-jerry-muskrat:
Thornton W. Burgess wrote The Adventures of Jerry Muskrat, one of his animal tales for children set around the Smiling Pool. Chapter one, Jerry Muskrat Has a Fright, opens with Jerry on the Big Rock, kicking his heels.

Jerry tries to recall what his mother said about Farmer Brown's boy and his traps, but he had half listened at the time. He puffs out his chest and vows he can fool any trapper, proud of once tricking the boy with a trout tale. Peter Rabbit then pops up with fresh word of traps set that night. Readers get pond life, pride, and peril, as a young muskrat learns care the hard way.
the-bat:
Mary Roberts Rinehart and Avery Hopwood built a mystery around a criminal known only as the Bat. Chapter one opens with a tired police chief pounding a table and ordering his detectives to get the man or fail. Gunmen and murderers, they feel, can be caught in time, but not this one.

Contents name Miss Van Gorder, pistol practice, a gathering storm, and Detective Anderson taking charge. A shot in the dark, a phone call from nowhere, a blackened bag, and handcuffs follow. A hidden room, an arrest, and still more murder lead to a final reveal and, in the last heading, quite a collection.
the-bobbsey-twins-on-a-houseboat: Laura Lee Hope wrote The Bobbsey Twins on a Houseboat. The front pages name her other sets, the Moving Picture Girls and the Outdoor Girls among them. In the Bobbsey list this book sits sixth, after tales in the country, at the shore, at school, and at Snow Lodge, and before the Meadow Brook book. The page that should list the parts is blank here, and no page of the tale is shown. The title alone sets the scene: four twins on a boat that is also a home.
the-desert-of-wheat:
Zane Grey's The Desert of Wheat, dated 1919, opens late in June in the vast northwestern wheat country. The grain begins to take on a tinge of gold. It spreads across an endless, rolling world of treeless hills, where miles of fallow ground and miles of waving grain slope up to far-separated farm homes.

Those homes look lost, mere dots on distant hills, amid broad squares of gold and brown reaching to the horizon. Grey calls it a lonely, hard, heroic country with no flowers, fruit, birds, brooks, or green pastures. Half of every hill is wheat and half is fallow; whirling strings of dust loop over the bare ground while the short, dry wheat lies back from the wind. Over all hovers a shadow that is neither dust nor gold, but lonely, waiting, and prophetic.
the-fern-lover-s-companion-a-guide-for-t:
George Henry Tilton wrote The Fern Lover's Companion as a guide to the ferns of the northeastern states and Canada. Alice D. Clark cut the pictures, and the book is given to her in thanks.

A key to the fern families comes first, then a plain scheme of how ferns are sorted. Groups follow: the polypodies, the bracken group, lip ferns, cloak ferns, chain ferns, and the spleenworts. Hart's tongue and walking leaf get their own place. Tilton wrote for walkers and plant lovers, not just scholars, so a reader can name a fern found on a rock or in deep woods.
the-go-ahead-boys-and-the-racing-motor-b: Ross Kay wrote The Go Ahead Boys and the Racing Motor-Boat. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page, the author's preface, and a contents list. Kay says every normal boy loves a motor-boat. A racer is loved most of all. He says facts lie behind the tale. The contents run from The Start and John Disappears. They run through The Missing Bag, An Upset, and A Rescue. They end with Sam's Warning. The heads promise races, rescues, and trouble on the water.
the-gold-bat: P. G. Wodehouse wrote The Gold Bat. The book is dated 1904. It is dedicated to Herbert Westbrook, called a prince of slackers. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list. The heads open with The Fifteenth Place and The Gold Bat. They turn to a mayor's statue and a league's warning. Later heads name house-matches, victim number three, and a white figure. They name a sprain and the Ripton match, in a school story of sport and pranks.
the-moving-picture-girls-at-sea-or-a-pic:
Laura Lee Hope's The Moving Picture Girls at Sea carries the subtitle A Pictured Shipwreck That Became Real. Only title page and the start of its contents are present here. The film story itself does not appear. The World Syndicate Publishing Company issued the volume at Cleveland and New York, with copyright by Grosset and Dunlap in 1915. A frontispiece shows Russ filming a pitching, tossing schooner.

Only five chapters are listed before the pages end. The Great Marine Film opens at page 1, followed by Jack Jepson and Something of a Mystery. The Sailor's Story and The Mary Ellen complete the visible list. Hope is billed as author of the Bobbsey Twins and Outdoor Girls series.
the-pursuit-of-the-house-boat: John Kendrick Bangs continues his house-boat fantasy in the Harper and Brothers edition of 1919, with Sherlock Holmes leading the Associated Shades. Twelve chapters move from the shades taking action through a stranger's revelations, a search party, conferences on deck and below stairs, and the chartering of a second vessel. Only the title pages and full contents list are present here, so the chase itself does not appear. The same contents appear in the companion 1897 record of the work.
the-railroad-builders-a-chronicle-of-the:
John Moody surveys a century of American railroad building. Yale University Press issued his volume in 1919. It belongs to the Chronicles of America series. His first chapter credits two inventions with remaking the United States. Farm machinery opened the land. The railroad carried crops to distant markets.

Chapters follow the Commodore and the New York Central. They cover the Pennsylvania and Erie systems. They cross the Appalachians and link the oceans. They reach the Pacific Northwest and the Santa Fe trail. Hill lines, Southern roads, and Edward H. Harriman follow. A closing chapter faces the American railroad problem. A bibliography ends the volume.
the-scapegoat:
Hall Caine's The Scapegoat opens with a preface and a long contents list. The chapters follow Israel ben Oliel and Naomi. She is born, grows up, and receives a great gift. She also suffers blindness, in the chapter headings. Israel journeys, is imprisoned, and returns. The Sultan enters, and the Mahdi comes, near the close.

Caine's preface describes a land within sight of an English port. English ships pass it on their way east, he says. Life there remains as it was a thousand years ago, in his telling. Government is oppression and law is tyranny there. Justice is bought and sold. It is a terror to be rich and a danger to be poor, he writes. The preface breaks off as it begins to name that land.
the-story-of-a-china-cat: Laura Lee Hope's Make Believe story of a china cat was published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York, illustrated by Harry L. Smith. Only the title pages and a publisher's list are present here. The list shelves the book among the Make Believe stories. The Sawdust Doll and the Nodding Donkey stand beside it. The Lamb on Wheels and the Calico Clown follow. The china cat's own adventures do not appear.
the-submarine-boys-on-duty-life-on-a-div: Victor G. Durham's first book of the Submarine Boys series, dated 1909 and subtitled Life on a Diving Torpedo Boat, introduces Jack Benson's ambition. Only the title page appears here, with two other pieces. A contents list of twenty-four chapters stands first. The first lines of chapter one follow. Jack asks whether this is Dunhaven. Jabez Holt answers slowly from his chair. The titles promise a fighting chance, thieves falling out, nerves tried under water, and a dive like magic, so the boys' service itself does not appear.
the-swoop-or-how-clarence-saved-england-:
P. G. Wodehouse published this tale of the great invasion in 1909, and his preface, signed from a bomb-proof shelter in London, mocks the invasion-scare literature it imitates. Some readers may think his colours too lurid, Wodehouse concedes. He has painted the horrors of a foreign invasion. England must still wake to her peril, he insists. Patriotism and duty alone made him write the story.

Part one opens on August the first in an English boy's home. Clarence Chugwater is a sturdy lad of about fourteen. He wears a flat-brimmed hat and a coloured handkerchief. He looks around him with a frown. He grits his teeth. He moans for England, his England. Wodehouse's deadpan heroics promise a comic antidote to the earnest invasion novels of the day.
the-tides-of-barnegat:
F. Hopkinson Smith's Tides of Barnegat opens some fifty years before its telling, on a spring morning along the New Jersey shore. Sunshine turns the road from Warehold village to Barnegat Light to satin, the marshes to velvet, and the stunted pines to bands of purple. Martha Sands, the Cobdens' nurse, is out with her dog Meg, leading the little creature down to bathe at the inner beach, her fine-weather custom.

The contents promise a doctor's gig, little Tod Fogarty, Ann Gossaway's red cloak, a spread of fire, high water at Yardley, and the claw of the sea-puss. Smith, a celebrated engineer-storyteller, builds a village novel where tides govern fortunes. Readers get a beloved nurse, a great house, and a shore community whose secrets will ebb and flood across twenty-two chapters.
the-world-s-fair-or-children-s-prize-gif:
The World's Fair, a children's prize gift book from London publishers Thomas Dean and Son, describes the Great Exhibition of 1851. Its subtitle promises accounts of inventions and manufactures shown there. Pretty stories about the makers are also promised. Readers learn how those makers live at home. The opening pages admire a picture of the exhibition building in Hyde Park. That structure, the book notes, is built of iron and glass.

Victorian children thus toured the famous Crystal Palace exhibition in print. Exhibits from many nations stood inside its glass walls. The book mixes wonder at new machines with human stories. Industry becomes a subject fit for young readers. It preserves how 1851's great show was explained to children at the time.
two-thousand-miles-on-an-automobile-bein: Two Thousand Miles on an Automobile, dated 1902, hides its author behind the name Chauffeur. The narrative promises a trip through New England, New York, Canada, and the West, with eighteen illustrations by Frank Verbeck. The contents move from the machine used to Ohio, Buffalo, western New York, and the Mohawk Valley. Only the front matter and contents are present here, so the road narrative itself does not appear.
uncle-sam-s-boys-with-pershing-s-troops-:
H. Irving Hancock's Uncle Sam's Boys with Pershing's Troops sends Dick Prescott to war against the Boche. The contents run from training camp through German spies in camp, conscientious objectors, and orders for over there. A troopship, sea wolves, no man's land, and a German prison camp fill the middle chapters.

Chapter one opens at training camp with a gray-haired colonel addressing his officers. Their task, he declares, is to produce the finest fighting army in the world with the least possible delay. His own Ninety-ninth regiment must become the finest in that army. Hancock wrote the series for boys following the American expeditionary force to France.
unknown-mexico-volume-1-of-2-a-record-of: Carl Lumholtz wrote Unknown Mexico. This first volume carries a long subtitle. It records five years of exploration among the tribes of the western Sierra Madre, in the Tierra Caliente of Tepic and Jalisco, and among the Tarascos of Michoacan. He dedicated the work to Morris K. Jesup, president of the American Museum of Natural History. The pages present here hold front matter only. They give the title page, the dedication, and a list of expedition papers. The travel narrative itself is not shown.
